text: From John A. Dix to Abraham Lincoln, May 9, 1863 The following Telegram received at Washington 925 PM. May 9 1863, From Fortress Monroe Dated, May 9 1863. I send in haste upon the boat our cable being broken a dispatch from Col. Kilpatrick Containing all the information I am able to obtain.1 1 Lincoln had telegraphed Dix and inquired whether any of the railroad bridges between Fredericksburg and Richmond had been destroyed. I only burned them over the Chickahominy— I do not know that he succeeded but was told by prisoners that he did.2 2 For more on the bridges, see Dix to Lincoln, May 11, 1863. (Signed) J. Kilpatrick” Col &c Jno. A. Dix Maj Genl.

text: From Robert H. Milroy to Abraham Lincoln, September 20, 1863 Washington City D. C. Sept. 20th 1863. Dear Sir, There has not yet been any announcement, official or otherwise, of any decision upon the evidence befor the Court of Inquiry in which I was concerned, In the multiplicity of your duties, this matter may have escaped your notice, The treatment I have received from my Government. by being suspended from command at the most important crisis of the country, & placed in arrest, and the continuance of that arrest for three months up to the present time without any explanation, have ocasioned me so much misery, that if made aware of it, I am sure you would not, from your known kindness of heart, withold what relief would be afforded me by the termination of my suspense as to your decision, and as to whether I am to be restored to command or not,1 1 For Lincoln's opinion, see his October 27, 1863 memorandum in this collection. With Great Respect Your Most Obt. Svt. R. H. Milroy M. G.

Dole to Abraham Lincoln, October 6, 1863 New York 6th Oct 1863 Dear Sir The inclosed letter reachd me here last night—1 I shall be detained here a few days & therefore send it to you as Senator Pomeroy evidently wishes you to know his views— As it is marked “private” to me, I leave you to judge as to its use other than for your own eye— After having spent a month or more in Kansas — and having been some time in Mo & Ill I found it impossible to make up my own mind as to the dificulties in Mo— In Kansas they are purely political— It is not entirely so in Mo there is an honest and earnest party there who believe that Scofield and those acting with him are to conservative to ever put down the rebellion— Kansas and Mo I think aught to be seperated— Kansas should have a commander not connected with their state politics— Mo requires a strong hand to control her people 1 Samuel C. text:
St. Louis
Feby. 24th 1862
To
His Excellency Abraham Lincoln
President of the United States of America -
Sir:
As
a member of the St. Louis Bar, & a citizen of the West,
I naturally feel a professional, & a public interest,
in the matter of the appointment of the Federal Circuit
Court Judge for the District, including the State
of Missouri. Allow me, therefore, to express to you
the satisfaction it would give me, if his honor,
Judge David Davis, of the State of Illinois, should
receive this appointment. I do not personally
know him, but his judicial, as well as personal,
reputation, has long made me hold him
in great estimation, & to value his fitness for
this high office to such a degree, as to make me
feel justified in expressing to you the
wish & hope, that he will be honored with
your nomination of him for it.
Very Respectfully yours
A. Todd
[*14649*]

text: From Daniel Butterfield to Abraham Lincoln, June 4, 1863 The following Telegram received at Washington 6.20 PM. June 4” 1863, From Hd Qrs Army Potomac Dated, June 4th 1863. Richmond Sentinel June 3d says — Jackson June 1st, Grant demanded the surrender of Vicksburg on Thursday giving three days to Pemberton1 to consider the demand. Pemberton replied that he did not want 15 minutes & that his troops would die in the trenches before they would surrender. The federal troops are demoralized & refused to renew the attack on Saturday. The enemys Gunboats are firing hot shot at the city the federal loss is estimated at 25.000 or 30.000 including Genl Kerr, Lay, Burbidge, Bonan, & one other. Port Hudson is invested Nothing in Enquirer of June 4”.2 1 John C. Pemberton was commander of the Confederate garrison at Vicksburg. 2 Lincoln replied by informing Butterfield that the information from the Richmond Sentinel was “greatly if not wholly incorrect.” See Collected Works, VI, 247. Danl Butterfield M. G.

text: From Horatio Seymour to Abraham Lincoln [With Endorsement by Lincoln]1, May 13, 1863 1 Dr. John Swinburne had offered his services to the War Department as a volunteer surgeon, with the endorsement of both New York's sitting and former governor. When his services were refused, Swinburne complained to Lincoln. On May 12, Lincoln wrote to Seymour and informed the governor that Swinburne could volunteer his services if the governor so desired. See Edwin D. Morgan to Edwin M. Stanton, May 5, 1863 and Collected Works, VI, 211. The following Telegram received at Washington 10.30 AM May 13 1863, From Albany NY Dated, May 13 1863. I have great Confidence in Dr. Swinbourn's skill but I Cannot ask the Gov't. to violate its rules. You know best the interest of the Army & I shall be Contented with Your decision— I am obliged to you for your Courtesy. Horatio Seymour Gov. of N. Y. [Endorsed on Envelope by Lincoln:] Gov. Seymour.

text: From William H. Seward to Abraham Lincoln, June 13, 1863 To the President: The Secretary of State, to whom was referred the Memorial of Franklin M. Seixas, relative to fifty-two bales of cotton seized at Lamar, Texas, taken to New York and condemned as prize, has the honor to report that although the question involved seems more properly to belong to the Navy Department, it may be remarked that the statements of the Memorialist are entirely exparte and unsupported by other proof. Assuming their correctness, however, by the claimant's own confession, he went to Texas for the purpose of clandestinely removing the cotton thence in violation of the blockade of the coasts of that State, of the laws of the United States, and the Regulations of the Treasury Department for trade in cotton. Under these circumstances, the Secretary of State does not see any sufficient ground for the interference of the Executive in the sale of the cotton for the benefit of the captors and of the United States. Respectfully submitted: William H. Seward, Department of State, Washington, 13th June, 1863.

text: From Abraham Lincoln to Henry W. Halleck [Copy in a Secretarial Hand]1, September 15, 1863 1 During the Fall of 1863 the Army of the Potomac was engaged in maneuvering against General Lee, but without expectation of a major battle. Generals Halleck and Meade, and the president, sought an opportunity to cut off a portion of Lee's army by a raid, if the opportunity should present itself. See Collected Works, VI, 450-51n. Executive Mansion, Washington, September 15, 1863. If I did not misunderstand Gen. Meade's last despatch, he posts you on facts as well as he can, and desires your views and those of the Government, as to what he shall do. My opinion is that he should move upon Lee at once in manner of general attack, leaving to developments whether he will make it a real attack. I think this would develop Lee's real condition and purposes better than the cavalry alone can do. Of course my opinion is not to control you and Gen. Meade. Yours truly [Endorsed on Envelope by Lincoln:] To Gen. Halleck.

text: From Salmon P. Chase to Abraham Lincoln, September 12, 1863 Sep. 12, 1863 My dear Sir, I enclose the letter of Col. Webster sent open to me that I might read it.1 1 See Edwin H. Webster to Lincoln, September 12, 1863. You will see that Col. Webster claims an assurance of yours, which he must be mistaken about. When neither the President nor the Secretary of the Treasury has the knowledge of a person clearly fitted for any office within the District of a Member of Congress, it is certainly expedient that the Member should be consulted: but he can have no right to any controlling voice. To recognize such a right would be to make the officers of the Government dependants of the Member and no Department & least of all the Treasury Department could be successfully administered on that theory. Very truly yours S P Chase

text:
From Thomas A. Scott to George B. McClellan, February 25, 1862
Received in cipher
Washington Feb 25 '62
Thirty six miles from Nashville 23d
Bowling Green 25th
To Major Genl G B McClellan
Nashville all right— Men wearied by excessive marching and toil— Before Columbus or Memphis is struck the Rebel army of over forty thousand men in Middle Tennessee should be crushed— To do this safely a little time must be given— Large detachments, we believe from rumors that reach us have left Manassas — of the truth of which you of course know Gen Buell and Halleck can effect the capture or surrender of Columbus and Memphis as early as they have secured the other important positions of the enemy— Give them help in the shape of good soldiers and you are certain to achieve great results—
T. A. Scott
Asst Secy of War

text: From George G. Meade to Henry W. Halleck, June 28, 1863 Received 10. A. M. Frederick Md. June 28, 1863 The order, placing me in Command of this army is received—1 As a soldier I obey it, and, to the utmost of my ability will Execute it— Totally unexpected as it has been, and, in ignorance of the Exact condition of the troops, and position of the enemy, I can only now say that it appears to me I must move toward the Susquehanna, Keeping Washington and Baltimore well covered, and if the enemy is checked in his attempt to cross the Susquehanna, or if he turns towards Baltimore to give him battle. I would say, that I trust Every available man that can be spared, will be sent to me, as from all accounts the enemy is in strong force— So soon as I can post myself up, I will communicate more in detail— 1 General Orders No. 194, dated June 27, 1863, removed Joseph Hooker from command of the Army of the Potomac and replaced him with General Meade. George G. Meade Maj Gen—

text: From David Hunter to Abraham Lincoln, June 30, 1863 Girard House, Philadelphia, June 30. 1863. Dear Sir: I have been deeply mortified at your implied censure, in relieving me from the command of the Depart. of the South. I feel confident I have done my whole duty, and that your Excellency has been deceived with regard to my course. This is no time for recriminations, and I beg you will at once give me a command, where I can prove myself not unworthy of your confidence, or order a Court to investigate my whole conduct.1 1 Hunter did not return to the field until May 1864 when he was given command of the Department of West Virginia. I have the honor to be, Very Respecty Your mo. ob. serv. D: Hunter Major Gen.

text: From Andrew H. Foote to Abraham Lincoln, March 13, 1862 Washington City, 14 Mar: 1862 Telegram in Cipher. “Cairo. 13 March. 11. P. M. ‘The iron-clad boats cannot be held when anchored by the stern in this current on account of the rods between the fantails forming the stern which yaws them about; and as the stern of the Boats are not clad and have but two 32 pounders astern, you will see our difficulty of fighting down stream effectually. Neither is there power enough in any of them to back up stream, we must therefore, tie up to the shore the best way we can, and help the Mortar boats. I have long since expressed to General Meigs my apprehensions about these boat's defects. Dont have any Gun boats for Rivers built with wheels amidships, as the drift-wood would take the wheel even if it had a powerful Engine! I feel it my duty to state these difficulties which could not be obviated when I came here, as the vessels were modelled and partly built. A. H. Foote Flag Officer”

President I find upon full inquiry that the report from Leavenworth to the effect that Union families have been driven out of Missouri is a gross misrepresentation & exageration A few men who claim to be loyal but who have been engaged in murder, robbery & arson have been driven out Their leader is Jos. Barnes whom you pardoned at the request of Gov Gamble1 & who is now trying to overthrow the state Govt. This Barnes & others of like character manufactured the excitement in Leavenworth & the false report sent to you. It is a base attempt of my enemies to influence your action 1 Hamilton R. Gamble Jas. Schofield Maj Genl

text: From Sidney Breese to Abraham Lincoln1, September 11, 1863 1 Breese, an Illinois lawyer and Democratic politician, was a member of the U. S. Senate (1843-49) and a justice of the Illinois State Supreme Court from 1857 until his death in 1878. Mt. Vernon Ill. Sept. 11. 1863 Dear Sir Engaged here for some days, in pouring over court records and examining law books, my attention was attracted to an editorial in the Missouri Republican, of yesterday, entitled, “Fraternizing”. It closes with a sentence from your inaugural address, which I had not recollected. I am so delighted with it, I send it to you with the expression of my opinion that a more beautiful idea, more beautifully expressed, cannot be found in any writer, ancient or modern. This is all I have to say at present, except to say I am your friend as ever. Sidney Breese

text:
ORDER OF PROCEEDINGS
OF THE
TWO HOUSES OF CONGRESS
ON THE
TWENTY-SECOND DAY OF FEBRUARY, INSTANT.
At one o'clock precisely the Senate will proceed to the Hall of the House of
Representatives, with invited guests, in the following order :
The Vice-President of the United States and the Secretary of the Senate,
preceded by the Sergeant-at-Arms.
Senators.
The President and Heads of the several Departments.
The Chief Justice and Associate Justices of the Supreme Court of the
United States.
Representatives from Foreign Governments, near this Government.
Invited Officers of the Army and Navy.
Distinguished Citizens, and other Invited Guests.
Preparatory to proceeding to the Hall of the House of Representatives, the
President and Heads of Departments will assemble in the President's Chamber ;
the Diplomatic Corps in the marble chamber in the rear of the Senate Chamber ;
the Justices of the Supreme Court in the Vice-President's Chamber ; invited
Army and Navy Officers in the Room of the Supreme Court, (the old Senate
Chamber ;) and distinguished citizens, and others invited, in the Senate Reception
Room.
PROCEEDINGS IN THE HALL OF REPRESENTATIVES.
PRAYER BY THE CHAPLAIN.
READING OF WASHINGTON'S FAREWELL ADDRESS.
After which, Flags captured from the Rebels will be presented from the Army
and Navy Departments to Congress.
Entrance to the Capitol will be found by the North and East doors of the
Senate wing, and by the East and West doors of the House wing. All other
means of access will be closed.
WASHINGTON, February 20, 1862.
[*14609*]

Received
Washington March 1st 62
From Harpers Ferry 12 M -
Genl R B Marcy -
More exact inquiry of the refugees produces
this report: -The Rebels moved their baggage
yesterday to Middleburg on Little River
turnpike - it was said the troops would
move today - Two reports were circulated
as to the destination - The prevailing one
was Winchester - The other that, relieved of
their baggage they would make a stand
at Leesburg or go to Manassas - The position
on Middleburg would strongly indicate
Winchester as their destination- Refugees
from W. this morning report that reinforcements
had been expected for a week but had
not yet arrived -
N P Banks
Major Genl Comdg

From William S. Rosecrans to Abraham Lincoln, May 27, 1863
The following Telegram received at Washington 1150 P.M. May 27. 1863,
From Murfreesboro 1115 PM.
Dated, May 27 1863
According to our latest news Forrest's Hd Qrs. were at Spring Hill yesterday & moved to Rigg's Cross-Roads eighteen (18) miles S. West of here today.1

W. S. Rosecrans.
Maj. Genl

Marsh to Abraham Lincoln, October 5, 1863 Legation of the United States Turin Oct 5. 1863 Sir I have the honor to enclose herewith a letter from General Garibaldi1 and am with profound respect 1 Guiseppe Garibaldi had gained international fame for his efforts to unify Italy under a republican government. He lived briefly in New York during the 1850s and had many admirers in the United States and Great Britain. At the outbreak of the Civil War, Garibaldi was offered a commission as a major general in the Union Army. Garibaldi stipulated that he would accept the commission only if he were made the commander-in-chief of the army and President Lincoln immediately abolished slavery. These conditions could not be met and he remained in Europe where he continued his efforts to unify and republicanize Italy. See Garibaldi to Lincoln, August 6, 1863. your obedient servant George P. Marsh

text:
From David Tod to Edwin M. Stanton [With Endorsement by Lincoln]1, June 27, 1863
[Newspaper Clipping:]
CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN GOVERNOR TOD AND THE SECRETARY OF WAR AS TO THE PAY OF COLORED TROOPS.
The State of Ohio, Executive Department,
Columbus, June 27th, 1863.
For the Press.
To correct a misapprehension in the public mind as to the pay and allowance to be made colored troops, I ask you to publish the following telegraphic correspondence with the Secretary of War, viz:
Columbus, O., June 26, 1863.
Hon. E. M. Stanton, Secretary of War, Washington, D. C.:
The colored regiment is progressing handsomely. The men are expecting the usual pay and bounty allowed white soldiers — will they get it?
DAVID TOD, Governor.
[Answer.]
Washington, June 26, 1863.
Governor Tod:
A careful examination of the acts of Congress by the Solicitor of the War Department had led him to the conclusion that the Government can pay to colored troops only ten ($10) dollars per month and no bounty; a month's advanced pay will be authorized; colored troops must trust to State contributions and the justice of Congress at the next session. Upon this basis the organizations have been made elsewhere.
E. M. STANTON,
Secretary of War.
The friends of the policy of raising colored regiments have already made an appeal to the people of Ohio for voluntary contributions for the support of the families of colored men who may volunteer. This decision of the War Department renders it necessary to raise an additional sum, if the colored soldiers should have the same pay as the white. Upon this point, it is hoped there will be no difference of opinion. The colored soldier fills the place of a white man — his risks are as great, if not greater. He is credited to the State upon its quota, thus reducing the draft upon white men. He has proved himself to be a good soldier. Put him then upon an equality so far as dollars and cents are concerned.
Circular letters, with forms of subscription, have been sent to the several County Military Committees, thus affording a general opportunity for all to contribute to the fund.
The high character of Messrs. Dennison, Dorsey, Wright and Burr, (the committee selected to disburse the fund), for integrity and capacity, is a sure guarantee that not one dollar will be misappropriated. Remittances should be made directly to Dr. G. Volney Dorsey, State Treasurer. A full statement of the amounts received, from whom received, and how disbursed, shall be published to the world.
It can hardly be necessary to make any further appeal to the patriotic people of Ohio.
To enable me to speak with confidence to those inclined to volunteer, prompt action is indispensably necessary.
DAVID TOD,
Governor.
[Endorsed on Envelope by Lincoln:]
Proclamation / Gov. Tod

Morris to Abraham Lincoln, September 25, 1863 Washington City Sept 25th 1863 Sir I promised to return you my argument on yesterday, but as you had properly taken time for deliberation, I thought it would make no difference if I witheld it for a day or so to enable me to complete the argument upon the action of the Interior Department in regard to Indian reservations in Illinois. Thos Cottman

text: Abraham Lincoln, Memorandum on West Point Appointments1, March 14, 1862 1 One of the President's prerogatives was the appointment of cadets to the prestigious Military Academy at West Point. This memorandum shows that Lincoln used this prerogative with due deliberation, concerning himself chiefly with whose sponsorship he intended to honor, rather than the qualifications of the nominees. Executive Mansion March 14. 1862 Memorandum. To-day I nominated the ten cadets at large and one for the District of Columbia — for the year— I have concluded that the next three I nominate shall be as follows— One for Gov. Seward, One for Mr. Sec. Welles One for H. T. Duncan of Kentucky,2 his candidate's name being “Thomas Collins, Timberlake”3 I wish Mr. Nicolay to keep this, and call my attention to it when ever I have an appointment to make. 2 H. T. Duncan practiced law in Paris, Kentucky. 3 The editors of Collected Works could not determine that anyone named Thomas Collins or Thomas Collins Timberlake was appointed to the military academy. See Collected Works, V, 161n. A. Lincoln

text: From Abraham Lincoln to John M. Schofield [Copy in a Secretarial Hand]1, July 20, 1863 1 William McKee, an editor of the Missouri Democrat, was arrested for publishing Lincoln's May 27 letter to General Schofield (q. v.). Lincoln replies here to Schofield's summary of the case in Schofield to Lincoln, July 14, 1863. For more on the arrest of McKee, see Henry T. Blow to Lincoln, July 13, 1863; James O. Broadhead to Lincoln, July 14, 1863; and Collected Works, VI, 326 and 329. Copy Executive Mansion, Washington, July 20th, 1863. My Dear General I have received and read your letter of the 14th of July. I think the suggestion you make, of discontinuing proceedings against Mr. McKee, a very proper one. While I admit that there is an apparent impropriety in the publication of the letter mentioned without my consent or yours, it is still a case where no evil could result, and which I am entirely willing to overlook. Yours truly A. Lincoln [Endorsed by Lincoln:] To Gen Schofield

From Frank Henry to Abraham Lincoln, May 3, 1863
A correspondent of a Philadelphia paper who left the field at Chancellorville this morning at 11 o'clock, has just arrived. He says that Longstreet and Jackson's corps were driven this morning from the position they took from Howard on Saturday evening. The enemy were driven four miles. He represents the greatest enthusiasm as preavailing among the troops who charged upon the enemy cheering. Gen. Meagher is again wounded. The railroad has certainly been cut.1
Very Respectfully &c.
Frank Henry
Times.

text: From William W. Murphy to Abraham Lincoln, June 2, 1863 Frankfort M. June 2d 1863 Sir; I have the honour to enclose a copy of the “Neue Frankfort Zeitung” one of the leading German papers of this city, and a paper which has always boldly stood out for its advocacy of the American union.— In this, Your Excellency will find the publication in English and German of the expression of thanks of your Excellency to the Germans for their contributions of linen and lint for the Union army. Allow me also to state, that the Germans are highly pleased with the same and that it has contributed much to attach them in feeling still more to our glorious Union for the preservation of which, Germany has a strong desire and for which also, were it deemed practicable, thousands of volunteers would gladly enlist to go over and fight in the Federal army.— I have the honor to be with great respect, Sir, Your most obedient Servant William W Murphy U. S. Consul General

text:
From Joseph Hooker to Seth Williams1, March 14, 1862
Received 1. P. M.
Budds Ferry
March 14. 1862
One of my Negro spies reports that he went to the Rappahannock — saw large bodies of troops yesterday below Fredericksburg on the Carolina side of the river—. troops he says are concentrating there in good numbers— Entrenchments are being thrown up on the Race Course — a place it is said artillery commands the approach for a great distance — vicinity a level plain. The bridges about Fredericksburg are standing. The rebels expect a great battle there— The prominent citizens there have their goods packed ready for a move— This can be relied on—

text: From Moses H. Grinnell to Abraham Lincoln, March 20, 1862 New York 20 March 62 Dear Sir You may be assured that a great many of your friends in this city, have learned with pleasure that you have expressed yourself favorably to the restoration of Commodore Stringham1 to active service, and as we are informed there will soon be appointed four flag officers— We most respectfully solicit that he may be one of them— 1 Silas Stringham Commodore Stringham has hosts of friends in this city, and they feel that great injustice has been done him in the Navy Dept— No charges have been bro't against him and his friends are confident nothing can be to impair his position as an officer of high merit, and long experience as Commander. It is in our opinion wicked to cast such a brave man aside (one who for thirty five years has been a devoted — loyal officer), through the pique of some such officer in the Navy Dep't— Excuse the liberty I take in addressing you on this subject, but beleive me Very Truly Your obd't Sevt M. H. Grinnell

My Dear Sir,

Very Truly Yours
N. W. Edwards

text: From William S. Rosecrans to Abraham Lincoln1, September 21, 1863 1 The following is a report on the battle at Chickamauga. Rec'd 1245 P.M. In Cipher Chattanooga Tenn Sept 21st 9. AM 1863 After two days of the severest fighting I ever witnessed our right and centre were beaten; The left held its position until Sunset. Our loss is heavy and our troops worn down. The Enemy recieved heavy reinforcements Saturday night. Every man of ours was in action Sunday & all but one Brigade on Saturday Our wounded large compared with the killed— We took prisoners from two divisions of Longstreet2 We have no certainty of holding our position here.— If Burnside3 could come immediately it would be well, otherwise he may not be able to join us unless he comes on west side of river4 2 In September 1863, General James Longstreet was sent from Lee's Army of Northern Virginia with two divisions to reinforce General Bragg in the West. 3 Ambrose E. Burnside 4 For Lincoln's reply, see Collected Works, VI, 474. W. S. Rosecrans Maj Gen Com'd'g

text:
From Erastus Corning to Abraham Lincoln1, June 23, 1863
Sir,
Your communication of the 12th inst,2 addressed to the officers of the public meeting held in this City on the 16th Ult. over which I presided commenting upon and controverting certain positions in regard to Constitutional obligations & personal rights, set forth in the Resolutions adopted by that meeting, has been received.— I was absent when it reached this City or it would have been acknowledged at an earlier day.—
The special duty assigned to the officers of the meeting, I consider fulfilled in sending the resolutions by its direction to you.—
In view however of the importance of the principles involved, and the public shape this matter has assumed; I have deemed it proper to hand your communication to the Committee who reported the Resolutions, for such action as in their judgment, the case may seem to demand.—
With sentiments of high respect, I remain
Yours very truly
Erastus Corning
Albany June 23d 1863.

text: From Edwin M. Stanton to Abraham Lincoln, September 19, 1863 Washington City, September 19th 1863. Sir: In obedience to the requirement of your note of yesterday1 I have the honor to state as follows, Colonel George P. Ihrie was appointed an additional aid de camp upon the staff of Major General Halleck through a misapprehension as to that officer's wishes with regard to the appointment. Gen'l. Halleck however declined to take him upon his staff; and he was then assigned to Gen'l Grant, who became dissatisfied with him and dismissed him from his head quarters. 1 See Collected Works, VI, 465. I have the honor to be Sir, Very Respectfully, Your obd't. serv't. Edwin M Stanton

text:
From John M. Schofield to Abraham Lincoln, June 20, 1863
The following Telegram received at Washington 2 A. M. June 21st 1863,
From St. Louis—
Dated, June 20th 1863.
The action of the Missouri State Convention upon the Question of Emancipation will depend very much upon whether they can be assured that the action will be sustained by the General Government & the people protected in their slave property being during the short time that Slavery is permitted to exist. Am I authorized in any manner directly or indirectly to pledge such support & protection? This question is of such vital importance to the peace of Missouri that I deem it my duty to lay it before your Excellency, —1
very Resp'y—
J. M. Schofield
Maj. Genl
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: John M. Schofield to Abraham Lincoln, Saturday, June 20, 1863 (Telegram regarding emancipation in Missouri)

text:
From Preston King to Abraham Lincoln, March 12, 1862
Washington March 12. 1862
Dear Sir
The Bearer Mr. Pascal Plant1 of this City is introduced to me to day by a friend in whom I have some confidence— Mr. Plant has an invention which he supposes can with security to itself & its managers be navigated and can destroy any vessel whether Iron Clad or not— He tells me he has a model sufficient to show the plan & power of his invention which he desires to exhibit to the President presuming that in these times you will consider any proposition of this kind worth looking at long enough to form an opinion whether it is of any value or not— I take the liberty to give Mr. Plant this letter of introduction that you may see what his invention is—
Very Respectfully
Preston King

text: From James K. Moorhead et al. to Abraham Lincoln, June 17, 1863 The following Telegram received at Washington 1.15 A. M. June 18th 1863, From Pittsburg 10.30 P.M. Dated, June 17th 1863. The undersigned appointed by the Executive committee of public Public safety acting in pursuance of the repeated & earnest wishes of successive meetings of citizens request you to authorize Major Genl. Brooks to declare Martial Law—1 1 General William Brooks was commander of the recently formed Department of the Monongahela. This department and the Department of the Susquehanna were created on June 9, 1863, for the purpose of organizing the defense of Pennsylvania, Eastern Ohio and West Virginia against an expected Confederate invasion. Lincoln wrote to Moorhead that General Brooks had the authority to arrest persons who interfered with his ability to conduct military operations. See Collected Works, VI, 286. J. K Morehead W. Thaw R. Miller Jr Jas. Plummer James Park Jr.

text: From John A. McClernand to Abraham Lincoln, June 23, 1863 The following Telegram received at Washington 5.30 A. M. June 24th 1863, From Cairo— Dated, June 23d 1863. I have been relieved for an omission of my Adjutant Hear me.—1 1 On May 30, 1863, McClernand issued General Orders No. 72 which congratulated his corps for its role in the campaign against Vicksburg. In these general orders, McClernand referred to his May 22 assault upon the Confederate works as the “first and largest success achieved anywhere along the whole line of our army.” For this and other exaggerated, self-serving claims made in the congratulatory order, McClernand was relieved from his command on June 18. For more on this episode, see Official Records, Series I, Volume 24, Part I, 158-65. John A. McClernand.

text: From Benjamin Brewster to Abraham Lincoln, June 18, 1863 706 Walnut St. Philada 17 June 63 Dear Sir: First. I must thank you for your most opportune and conclusive paper on the subject of Military arrests.1 It is a triumphant vindication & will be read & understood by all men. 1 A reference to Lincoln's June letter to Erastus Corning and Others. A draft of the letter is in this collection. Second. Do not yield to importunities to send Genl. McClellan to Pennsylvania We want no such dead heads here. It would be a concession wrung from you that would be beneath your dignity & tarnish the honour of the country. Let us have Cadwalader2 & men here will be content 2 General George H. Cadwalader, a native of Pennsylvania, was given a command at Philadelphia in the recently created Department of the Susquehanna. I am with regard & respect Yr friend B. H. Brewster

text: From Eber B. Ward to Abraham Lincoln, July 11, 1863 Detroit July 11th 1863 Sir I see it stated that Seward proposes to settle with the southern traitors and practically give them all they ask. Their liberty & their property Such a settlement would ruin the hopes of the friends of the Administration, destroy the party that sustains you, sink Seward beneath the contempt of the meanest coward, and place the Copperheads1 of the north with the slaveholders of the south in power 1 “Copperhead” was a term used to refer to a Northerner who opposed the war or criticized the Lincoln administration. Rather than live to witness any other settlement than the unconditional surrender of the armed rebels and scoundrels, I would sink myself and my estate in the middle of the Ocean Every friend of you and your administration condemns without reserve the least inclination to such a surrender of the rights and interests of the north Respy E B Ward

text: From Edward Bates to Abraham Lincoln, February 18, 1862 1/2 past 2. p.m. Feb 18. 1862 Honored Sir, The papers sent over to me half an hour ago, being two letters & several rolls, numerously signed, all relate to Capt Nathaniel Gordon, now under sentence of death on a conviction of piracy, in the African Slave trade.1 1 After a temporary stay of execution issued by Lincoln on February 4, Gordon was executed on February 21. The papers, all of them, ask that Gordon's sentence be compute commuted to imprisonment for life. No reasons are given to shew a doubt of the guilt of the papers contain no suggestion of any impropriety in the legal proceedings. And these are the only papers in the case which I have seen. I see nothing in the papers, as presented to me, to make it proper for you to interfere, to stop the course of law I have the honor to be Most respectfully Your obt servt Edwd. Bates

text: From John M. Fleming and Robert Morrow to Abraham Lincoln, August 7, 1863 Washington, D. C, Aug. 7. 1863 Dear Sir:— For now three days we have unsuccessfully sought an opportunity to deliver to you, in person, a petition from the loyal people of East Tennessee1 (our own section) touching their present and prospective lamentable condition. We brought with us letters from Gen's Burnside and Carter2 seconding our mission, the former of which was sent in to your Excellency on Wednesday. It has been thought proper to accompany the delivery of said petition with some verbal explanations, and therefore it is that we seek a personal interview either this evening or to-morrow morning as to your Excellency may be the more convenient,3 1 See East Tennessee Citizens to Abraham Lincoln, July 1863. 2 Ambrose Burnside and Samuel P. Carter 3 A draft of Lincoln's August 9 reply to Fleming and Morrow is in this collection. Very Respectfully, Your Excellency's Obt Sevts, Jno: M. Fleming Ro. Morrow.

Washington Augt 9th 1863 254 F Street Sir I beg leave to tender my grateful acknowledgements for your kind consideration in directing that I should be relieved from the order under which I was mustered out of the service in April last, and for your special order, restoring my date pay and emoluments. But on account of the stringency of the certificate which requires me to state that I have been regularly stationed on duty at Washington during the period charged for, I cannot sign it. I believe myself entitled to this allowance, and respectfully ask that the Quarter Master at this Station (Major Morris S Miller) may be authorized to pay me on a certificate in which this phrase may be omitted. I am With high consideration and Sincere regards Your very obedt Servant Charles F Havelock

text: From Samuel Galloway to Abraham Lincoln, February 28, 1862 Columbus Feby 28 1862 My dear friend I observed in yesterdays (Thursdays Cincinnati Commercial under in the column containing the notices of Congressional proceedings the statement “that the Army Committee have agreed to report in favor of a National foundry East of the Alleghanies and armory foundry and manufacturing arsenal west of the Alleghanies the sites of all to be made by five Commissioners appointed by the President”. I write to state that if Congress should adopt the Report of the Committee I would be gratified to be appointed one of the Commissioners I have no partialities nor prejudices to gratify, nor any selfish object or interest to be accomplished. I think that I could discharge such a trust with impartiality and might be useful to the country in Executing so important a commission as that contemplated. Receive my congratulations on the prospect of a restoration of the health of Mrs Lincoln & Tad— As Ever Yours &c Saml Galloway

text:
From Mark W. Delahay to Abraham Lincoln, June 19, 1863
Leavenworth, Kan. June 19th 1863
Dear Lincoln
I have read all Your letters and speeches and am sure Your letter to Mr Corning & others1 is the best thing of all, because it annihilates the clamor and pretended wrong done to a notable Ohio Traitor, it will be the best document that can be circulated this year, Ohio aught to have millions of them printed an circulated, I have just ordered Ten Thousand for more Extended Circulation in Kansas— You undoubtedly will be blamed for making two few arrests of Northern traitors & I must be Excused when I say You are too Easy and lennient with that class, and Traitor News papers—
Very Truly Yours
M W Delahay

text:
From Elisha Whittlesey to Abraham Lincoln1, March 12, 1862
Treasury Department
Comptrollers Office
March 12th 1862—
My Dear Friend
As I was leaving the office yesterday at Four oclock, I received Your esteemed favor of that date, requesting if any accounts from the mansion should appear wrong to make it known to You, directly.2
I have been deterred from communicating with you personally, on that; and on other subjects, from my knowledge of the weighty matters, that engross Your attention.
If You have a constituent or fellow citizen, more sincerely devoted to You than myself, I am not aware of it. Your request shall be observed.
Most Respectfully
and Sincerely
Yours—
Elisha Whittlesey—

M. 3rd In Cipher Memphis May 2nd 1863 12. noon I learn from two independent sources that Col Grierson1 has passed below Jackson Miss, cut the Railroad at Hazelhurst & destroyed fifty thousand 50000 pounds of Bacon and an Ammunition train and is on his way down to Baton Rouge to join General Banks.2 I believe it to be true as my orders were to push South if safer than to come north 1 Benjamin H. text: From Benjamin B. French to Abraham Lincoln, July 7, 1863 July 7th. 1863 1/2 past 4. p. m. My Dear Sir, The Bearer is Col. J. A. Peck who has just called on me to aid him in procuring a Band to serenade you this evening, in congratulation of the glorious news recd. today.1 1 On July 7, news reached Washington that Vicksburg had surrendered on July 4. Lincoln was serenaded on the evening of July 7 and made a speech at the occasion. For Lincoln's remarks, see Collected Works, VI, 319-20. The Col. calls to ask you to remain at the Presidential mansion & receive the Serenade. All Washington will join in the congratulation, as I do most heartily. May God bless our Union & our President! Sincerely yours B. B. French

text:
From Abraham Lincoln to Oliver O. Howard [Draft]1, July 21, 1863
Executive Mansion,
Washington, July 21, 1863.
My dear General Howard
Your letter of the 18th is received— I was deeply mortified by the escape of Lee across the Potomac, because the substantial destruction of his army would have ended the war, and because I believed, h such destruction was perfectly easy — believed that Gen. Meade and his noble army had expended all the skill, and toil, and blood, up to the ripe harvest, and then let the crop go to waste— Perhaps my mortification was partly heightened because I had always believed — making my belief a hobby possibly — that the main rebel army going North of the Potomac, could never return, if well attended to; and because I was so greatly flattered in this belief, by the operations at Gettysburg— A few days having passed, I am now profoundly grateful for what was done, without criticism for what was not done— Gen. Meade has my confidence as a brave and skillful officer, and a true man.
Yours very truly
A. Lincoln

text: From William H. Ludlow to Edwin M. Stanton1, June 29, 1863 1 Colonel William Ludlow was the Federal agent for the exchange of prisoners. Received 8.30 P. M. June 29 Fort Monroe June 29, 1863 I am making every effort for release of Richardson & Browne.2 2 Lincoln had written to Ludlow on June 1 and asked him to try and secure the release of Junius Browne and A. D. Richardson. Browne and Richardson were reporters for the New York Tribune who had been captured near Vicksburg. As of December 1864, Browne and Richardson were still imprisoned at Richmond. For Lincoln's letter to Ludlow, see Collected Works, VI, 241. My first application was refused peremptorily— I have made another, The result of which I shall know & report on the return of the flag of truce boat from City Point on Thursday. They are held in retaliation for citizens arrested & held by us. This is the assigned reason the real reason I believe to be that they are connected with the Tribune and are held to annoy. Wm. H. text:
From John Hay to Abraham Lincoln, October 4, 1863
Columbus, Ohio,
October 4, 1863.
Dear President:
An accident detained me in Columbus today and gave me an opportunity of seeing Brough.1
He requests me to apologize for his seeming rudeness in not answering your letter,2 and hopes that the verbal reply sent by Govr. Dennison3 was entirely satisfactory.
He says they will carry Ohio by at least 25,000 votes, independent of the soldiers who will indefinitely increase it.4 The Vallandigam5 men have given up the fight here.
Brough is much more anxious about Curtin6 than about himself.
Brough thinks that as yet in the Keystone State
The prospect is rather uncertain;
The fifth act is near, and we only can wait,
Impatient, the rise of the Curtin.
A hazy joke, with which I close.
Yours respectfully,
John Hay.

text:
Private Instructions to Presidents of County Clubs.
On a slip of paper heretofore sent-you will find the Entering
Password for the first quarter of 1862, marked 1 : the Retiring
Password, for the same quarter, marked 2 : the Traveling Password,
for the year 1862, marked 3 : the Rallying Cry, marked 4 : and the
Answer to the same, marked 5.
You will communicate these Passwords etc. to the Presidents of
Subordinate Clubs in your County.
These Passwords should be given to worthy members only, and
should be used only in a whisper. The Rallying Cry should be
given, to all worthy members, in a whisper, but is intended to be
used when occasion demands, aloud. When a member is attacked
or desires instant aid for any legitimate purpose he may shout the
Rallying Cry. If no aid reaches him within a reasonable time
he may repeat it. The Cry is to be answered by any member
hearing it, and aid is to be rendered without delay. The Presidents
of Clubs should not impart these Passwords etc. to any but members
of their own Clubs.
The Traveling Password should be given only to members about
to visit another State. The stranger who visits a Subordinate Club
outside of his own State will be waited upon by the President or
his representative, who will examine him in the manual or badge
signs, and see that he wears the badge authorized by his own State
Club. If correct the president will say ; " Have you the Traveling
Password?" He will reply ; "I have," and will give the first letter
of the word; the President will give the next, and so on alternately
until the whole word is spelled. No visitor from another State
should be admitted without this examination, nor unless he wears
the badge authorized by his own State Club.
The Executive Committee request the earnest and cordial co-operation
of the officers of Clubs throughout the State in effecting a thorough
reorganization of the Clubs, by disposing of all unworthy members,
by holding regular meetings and enlisting the aid and sympathy of
all unconditional Union men. We must present a solid front to the
enemies of our country, and be prepared to extend out work Southwardly
as soon and as rapidly as circumstances will permit.
[*14663*]
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: Lexington Kentucky Central Union Club, Thursday, February 27, 1862 (Circulars)

text: From John C. Forrest and Julian R. Campbell to Abraham Lincoln, June 10, 1863 Dear Sir, The Resolution enclosed, was passed unanimously, at a Meeting of the Grand State Council (in R. I.) of the Union League of America. I am directed by said Council to transmit a copy of the same to you. Very Respectfully Yours &c Jno. C. Forrest Grand President Providence R. I. June 10/63 Julian R. Campbell. Grand Recording & Cor. Sect'ry. [Attached Resolution:] Resolved! That this Grand State Counsel fully indorse and approve of the course adopted by the present Administration in issuing the Proclamation of Emancipation, in Confiscating the property of Rebels, and in Employing and arming Colored Citizens, to aid in Suppressing the rebellion. A true Copy attest Julian R. Campbell.1 1 John Hay wrote to Campbell on June 15 and thanked him on behalf of the president, for sending the above resolution. A draft of Hay's letter is in this collection. —Secy:—

text:
From John E. Wool to Edwin M Stanton, March 8, 1862
Received in cipher
Washington March 9th
10.20 AM
From Fortress Monroe 8th
The Merrimac came Down from Norfolk today and about two oclock attacked the Cumberland and Congress— She sunk the Cumberland and the Congress surrendered— The Minnesota is aground and attacked by the Jamestown, Yorktown and Merrimac— The Saint Lawrence just arrived and going to assist— The Minnesota is aground— Probably both will be taken — that is the opinion of Capt Marston and his officers— The Roanoke is under our guns— It is thought the Merrimac, Jamestown and Yorktown will pass the fort tonight—
John E Wool
Major Genl

text: From James H. Lane, Abel C. Wilder, and John Covode to Abraham Lincoln [With Endorsement by Lincoln]1, June 8, 1863 1 General James G. Blunt of the Department of Kansas had allowed two men to be hanged by a “citizens court” at Atchison, Kansas on May 23, 1863. Consequently Governor Thomas Carney of Kansas, who was already unfavorably disposed toward Blunt, demanded his removal from command. See Lincoln to James H. Lane, April 27, 1863, Blunt to Donald Carmichael, May 22, 1863, Blunt to Lincoln, June 9, 1863. Washington, June 8, 1863. Sir We have learned with pain & sorrow that charges have reached you calculated to prejudice our gallant young Maj Genl Blunt— Confident he can cleanse himself & reinstate himself in your good opinion — we respectfully request you to permit him to visit you at this city— Yours truly J. John Covode NB We make this application at the earnest request of Maj Genl Blunt— [Endorsed by Lincoln:] About Gen. Blunt.

text:
From John E. Wool to George B. McClellan, March 9, 1862
Washington Mar 9th
Fortress Monroe 6 PM
Two hours after my despatch to the Secy of War last evening the Monitor arrived— She immediately went to the assistance of the Minnesota aground & continued so until a few moments since— Early this morning she was attacked by the Merrimac Jamestown & Yorktown after a five hours contest they were driven off and the Merrimac in a sinking condition— She was towed by the Jamestown Yorktown & several smaller boats towards Norfolk no doubt for the purpose if possible to get her in the dry dock for repairs The Minnesota is afloat & being towed towards Fort Monroe— The arrival of the Monitor was fortunate indeed it saves not only the Minnesota but all the public property outside and probably that inside of the fort— It is reported by Genl Mansfield that he is menaced with an attack by land— I have sent him all my troops except 3 regiments besides a light battery of six pieces & a company of cavalry— He has about eight thousand effective men—
John E Wool
Major Genl
title: Abraham Lincoln papers: Series 1. General Correspondence. 1833-1916: John E. Wool to George B. McClellan, Sunday, March 09, 1862 (Telegram reporting engagement between Monitor and Merrimac)

text:
Edwin M. Stanton, Draft of General Orders1, May 13, 1863
Washington City,
May 13th 1863.
General Orders No.
Whereas C. L. Vallandigham has been arrested and is now held in Military custody as a prisoner by Major General Burnside under orders of the President of the United States; And whereas, in view of the existence of the present rebellion, in the judgment of the President, public safety requires the suspension of the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in the case of said Vallandigham, arrested as aforesaid.
Now, therefore, it is hereby ordered by the President that the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus, and any writ which has been or may be hereafter issued during the present rebellion in the case of said Vallandigham, be, and the same is hereby suspended.

text: From Horace Binney Jr. et al. to Abraham Lincoln, June 16, 1863 The following Telegram received at Washington 5 PM. June 16 1863, From Philadelphia 4 PM. Dated, June 16 1863. President Lincoln Cannot general Cadwallader be sent to Phila with orders to organize a force under the present head of this Dept for the present Emergency The people here want a leader whom they know & in whom they have confidence We do not desire to interfere with Genl Couch but Cadwallader is the man for Phila & awaits your orders1 1 Lincoln replied that he had sent General George Cadwalader to discuss this matter with Secretary Stanton and General Halleck. Darius N. Couch was commander of the recently created Department of the Susquehanna and Cadwalader was given a command in this department with his headquarters at Philadelphia. See Collected Works, VI, 279. Horace Binney Jr J E Thompson J J Clark Howe H. C. Carr M McMichael N B Browne W M Tilghman G H Baker O Gibbons

text: From Henry T. Blow to Abraham Lincoln [With Endorsement by Lincoln]1, May 5, 1863 1 For the petition in question, see St. Louis Citizens to Lincoln, April 30, 1863. The petition protested Governor Hamilton R. Gamble's authority to remove officers in the Missouri State Militia. St. Louis May 5. 1863 Sir: I have the honor to enclose a Petition from some of our best Union men, for which your careful consideration is requested. text: From Simon Cameron to Abraham Lincoln, June 29, 1863 The following Telegram received at Washington 840 PM. June 29th 1863, From Harrisburg Dated, June 29 1863. We have reliable and undoubted information from three distinct sources that General Lee now has nearly if not quite one hundred thousand (100000) men between Chambersburg on the Upper side of South Mountain and Gettysburg on the East side of the Mountain and the Susquehanna River— His columns at present extend from Shippensburg to near Harrisburg & from Gettysburg to near Columbia— They have over two hundred fifty (250) pieces of Artillery by actual count— Within the next forty eight 48 hours Lee will cross the Susquehanna River unless Genl Meade strikes his columns tomorrow & compels him to concentrate his forces west of the Susquehanna for a General Battle— Let me impress on you the absolute necessity of action by Meade tomorrow even if attended with great risk because if Lee gets his Army across the Susquehanna and puts our armies on the defensive at that time you will readily comprehend the disastrous results that must follow to the Country Simon Cameron

text: From George B. McClellan to Randolph B. Marcy, February 27, 1862 Copy Sandy Hook M'd February 27. 1862 It being impossible to build a bridge of canal boats — as well as impossible to unload and take across the river with sufficient promptness — the supplies needed by any large force, on account of the very limited space — I have determined to adopt the course I indicated to the President and Secretary of War — viz — to cover the opening of the Railway without — and the rebuilding of its bridges— In the mean time depots can be established which will make an advance easy— But this requires time— The fact that Canal boats could not be used, was ascertained only today — and I regarded the other projected operations as too important to be deferred for the time necessary to accomplish this, which can be done at any time thereafter the Railway being meanwhile opened— (Signed) G. B. McClellan Maj Gen'l Comd'g [Endorsed by Randolph B. Marcy:] The foregoing was received this morning R. B. Marcy Chief of Staff

From Abraham Lincoln to Andrew Johnson [Copy]1, September 19, 1863
Private
Executive Mansion
Washington, DC. Sept. 19. 1863
My dear Sir:
Herewith I send you a paper, substantially the same as the one, drawn up by yourself, and mentioned in your despatch, but slightly changed in two particulars— First, yours was so drawn as that I authorized you to carry into effect the fourth Section &c. whereas I so modify it so as to authorize you to so act as to require the United States to cary into effect that Section. Secondly, you had a clause committing me, in some sort to the State Constitution of Tennessee, which I feared might embarrass you in making a new constitution if you desire— So I dropped that clause.
Yours very truly
A Lincoln

text: From Joseph Hooker to Abraham Lincoln, July 7, 1863 Washington July. 7 1863. Mr President After having complied with my instructions on being relieved of the command of the Army of the Potomac I came to Washington for the purpose of seeking an interview with yourself and the Secretary of War. This morning I have been placed in arrest by order of the Major General Commanding the Army for visiting Washington without a pass. It is almost unnecessary for me to add that in my previous visits to this city this rule was never enforced in my case. Under the usages of service it is not considered proper to call on superior officers except with their consent and I therefore request that the his Excellency will have me informed whether or not he will grant me an audience for half an hour. And if so appoint the time I can have the honor of meeting him Very respectfully Your obt st Joseph Hooker Maj. Gnl.

text:
From Gustavus V. Fox to George B. McClellan, March 9, 1862
Received in Cipher
Washington Mar 9th 62
Fortress Monroe 9th eve—
Your telegram to Major Genl Wool received— The performance of the Monitor today against the Merrimac shows a slight superiority in favor of the Monitor as the Merrimac was forced to retreat to Norfolk after a four hours engagement; at times the vessels touching each other— The damage to the Merrimac cannot be ascertained— She retreated under steam without assistance— The Monitor is all ready for her tomorrow but I think the Merrimac may be obliged to lay up for a few days— She is an ugly customer and it is too good luck to believe we are yet clear of her— Our hopes are upon the Monitor and this days work shows that the Merrimac must attend to her alone— Have ordered the large frigates to leave—
G V Fox
Asst Secy

From William H. Seward to Abraham Lincoln [In Frederick Seward's hand; With Endorsement by Lincoln]1, June 10, 1863

My dear Sir:
In a note of a day or two since, I mentioned that I had made an appointment with Mr Molina for you to receive him at twelve today. When he called, however, he unfortunately found that you had gone out, undoubtedly because the appointment had escaped your recollection. Will you see him at the same hour tomorrow? If so he will be informed accordingly.
Faithfully Yours.
William H Seward
Department of State
10. June
Regretting my forgetfulness, of course I will see Mr Molina to-morrow.
A. Lincoln

Executive Mansion.
Washington. March 7. 1862.
My dear Sir:
Mr James F. B. Marshall of Mass. is now with me on the question of the Honolulu Commissioner. It pains me some that this tilt for the place of Col. Baker's3 friend grows so fierce, now the Col. is no longer alive to defend him. I presume, however, we shall have no rest from it— Mr Marshall appears to be a very intelligent gentleman, and well acquainted with the affairs of the Sandwich Islands. The California delegation also expect the places for some one of their citizens. In self-defence I am disposed to say — “Make a selection and send it to me.”
Yours truly.
A. Lincoln.

I hope you will find it beneficial. With good wishes & congratulations — I am Most respectfully— N Sargent

To Hon. E M Stanton Secty War
The Military work in Tennessee is nearly
complete- it is now important that a Military
[ ] should be appointed to organize
and act as Governor until the people can
have an opportunity to make nomination &
elect a Legislature- this may require considerable
time- when we occupy Memphis
and Knoxville and the people feel at liberty
to vote without military restraint- Tennessee
will at once wheel into the Union- the
moral effect of Tennessee again becoming
a member of the Union will be tremendous.
Governor Harris and his legislature have run
away- they adjourned last Sunday week to
meet in Memphis the 20th Up to this time

text: From William S. Rosecrans to Abraham Lincoln, October 3, 1863 In cipher The following Telegram received at Washington, 105 AM. Oct 4 1863. From Chattanooga Tenn 1 PM. Dated, Oct 3 1863 If we can maintain this position in such strength that the enemy are obliged to abandon their position, and the Elections in the Great States go favorably, would it not be well to offer a general amnesty to all officers and soldiers in the Rebellion? It would give us moral strength and weaken them very much.1 1 Lincoln responded on October 4, saying in part, that if the Union held Chattanooga and East Tennessee, “the rebellion must dwindle and die.” The President then gently urged Rosecrans to action. See Collected Works, VI, 498. W S Rosecrans Maj Genl

text:
Washington City
February 21, 1862
Honorable Chas Gibson:
My dear Sir:
After
mature reflection I am entirely satisfied
that as a great military measure, it were
advisable that the President should at
an early period authorize the extension
of the South West Branch of the Pacific
Rail Road from its present terminus,
Rolla to Springfield distant one hundred
& eighteen miles. Under the act of
Congress he could readily take this
road and place the same in the
care of the directors, authorizing them
to extend the same, and after consulting
with you, I am entirely satisfied
that the Contract motioned by us and
others consulted would accomplish
the purpose and be safe to the Government.
From your knowledge of the
directors, you could safely repose confidence
in their integrity and energy
and a faithful execution of the trust?
There is much of the work already
done and I am satisfied that a
good military rail road could be
built and finished for transportation
to Springfield in ten or twelve months
for the three millions specified in the
agreement or Contract?
From Rolla to the Little Piney, 12 miles
the road is nearly ready for the rails
and could be finished in a brief period.
[*14626*]

text:
The New-York Times,
York, where Anti-Slavery sentiment has not been used to flourish hardily.
The President on Emancipation.
If proof were wanting of the patriotic ardor
of the President for the peace and well
being of the country, it would be found
abundantly in the message sent yesterday to
Congress. Mr. LINCOLN appreciates the infinite
difficulty of the Slavery question. He
evidently despairs of prostrating the institution
by force of the war-power; he looks to
its existence in full vigor, throughout the Gulf
States at least, when the war shall have
ended. The utmost reach of his practical
dealing with the subject is to
strip it of political influence in National affairs.
To effect this capital object, there is
certainly no way so sure as to destroy the
identity of interest between Border Slave
States and those at the southward; and this
object the President's suggestion proposes to
attain. It takes the form of a joint resolution
submitted to the consideration of Congress.
The possibility of one or more States
discovering the impolicy of retaining slave-labor
is assumed. To such the joint resolution
offers pecuniary aid in the task of emancipation,
by engaging to pay a sum prefixed
for each enslaved negro set at liberty. This
bounty the President evidently believes will
turn the scale in favor of freedom. Satisfied
of the good faith of the National Government
in its professions of non-intervention in the
legislation of the States, the States will be
ready to look favorably upon a plan which,
while it makes the merit of the act of emancipation
their own, throws the cost elsewhere.
And as the plan is adopted, one after
another of the northerly Slave States will array
themselves on the side of the free communities
of the North.
In considering the Presidential project, a
number of difficulties will no doubt suggest
themselves to Congress. Any State disposed
to part with its negroes will naturally offer
them in the best market. The extreme South,
in the supposition raised by Mr. LINCOLN that
Slavery will there retain all its vitality, will
compete with the North in the purchase of
the discarded labor; and must of necessity
offer prices which the North will be unable to
pay. When peace shall be restored—always
assuming the President to be right in regard
to Slavery in the Gulf States—Kentucky will
be able to get $130,000,000 for her negroes at
the South, while the North, presupposing the
round price of $200—the highest rate heretofore
named, and considered practicable—would be
able to offer only one-third of that amount.
If by an act of gradual emancipation Kentucky
is thus able at any moment to get the
larger sum for her slaves, what temptation to
the passage of such an act will be the offer of
the smaller? Congress will also have to
weigh well that incessantly recurring question,
what shall be done with the negroes when
freed? Their freedom in any border State
will no doubt be followed by their expulsion.
Even from Illinois, Mr. LINCOLN's immediate
State, the blacks are about to be expelled.
Will it not be necessary for the National
Government to provide also for their removal
from the country, and their colonization and
christianization in a new and distant home?
And will not this cost, added to the other,
constitute a total from which the country,
already startled at the coming terror of war,
taxation, will draw back appalled?
We fear that the Presidential plan will not
achieve the good for which it is so patriotically
designed. It will not induce any Slave
State to discard Slavery; it will not, therefore,
weaken any of the ties between the collective
Slave States. It will offer no sufficient
reason for departing, even in appearance,
from the doctrine that, with
Slavery in the States, the National
Government has no concern whatever. It will
be attended with an expense too overwhelming
to be regarded favorably by a people who
have already upon their shoulders the burden
present and prospective of a debt of several
thousands of millions—a burden placed there
by Slavery. But let the plan have full discussion;
let it also have full credit, as evidence
that the Government contemplates no forcible
interference with the institutions of any State,
rebellious or loyal, and desirable good may
grow out of it.
[*14819-6*]

the passage of such an act will be the offer of
the smaller? Congress will also have to
weigh well that incessantly recurring question,
what shall be done with the negroes when
freed? Their freedom in any border State
will no doubt be followed by their expulsion.
Even from Illinois, Mr. LINCOLN's immediate
State, the blacks are about to be expelled.
Will it not be necessary for the National
Government to provide also for their removal
from the country, and their colonization and
christianization in a new and distant home?
And will not this cost, added to the other,
constitute a total from which the country,
already startled at the coming terror of war,
taxation, will draw back appalled?
We fear that the Presidential plan will not
achieve the good for which it is so patriotically
designed. It will not induce any Slave
State to discard Slavery; it will not, therefore,
weaken any of the ties between the collective
Slave States. It will offer no sufficient
reason for departing, even in appearance,
from the doctrine that, with
Slavery in the States, the National
Government has no concern whatever. It will
be attended with an expense too overwhelming
to be regarded favorably by a people who
have already upon their shoulders the burden
present and prospective of a debt of several
thousands of millions—a burden placed there
by Slavery. But let the plan have full discussion;
let it also have full credit, as evidence
that the Government contemplates no forcible
interference with the institutions of any State,
rebellious or loyal, and desirable good may
grow out of it.

text:
Annapolis, Md Feby 28 1862
To his excellency, Abraham Lincoln
President of the United States
Most Honored Sir:
Permit us
members of the legislature of the state of Maryland,
to present and introduce to your acquaintance and
patronage our friend and the friend of your administration,
Richard Chambers, a native of Maryland and long a
citizen of Caroline County.
In our opinion and belief we cannot introduce to
your notice a worthier man, or a more competent business
citizen than Mr. Chambers. He is widely known in
various states as the Publisher in 1842 of a selection of the
Hon. H Clay's speeches with the view of aiding the election
of Mr. Clay. Mr. Chambers was the friend and intimate
acquaintance of Mr. Clay and such was his confidence in
Mr. Chambers that, had he been elected, he promised
unasked by Chambers, an important place, on the contingency
of his election.
As a man and politician, he has borne the character
of a most candid man and those that have encountered
his pen have ever rued the contact. Mr. Chambers
defended the present Head of the government before
his election and has published many articles [?datory]
of his administration. A former [patriot?] [?] live
nor a more decisive union loving man.
[*14726*]

between Taylor's Battery and the right of Genl Smith, and
thus protected the left of the second line of battle from flank
attack.
While these movements were being executed, the sound of
Genl Smith's musketry was heard, indicating an attack upon
Redan No 1, in his front. Soon after Col. Webster, chief of your
staff, came with the welcome intelligence that the enemy had
retired, before the gallant and chivalrous assault of Genl. Smith,
and that he was already leading his men into this Redan, which
he firmly held.
Col. Webster also brought your order to press upon the
enemy at all points.
Genl Wallace, reporting through on of his officers that
he had met the enemy and was pressing him with success,
requested me to send forward 5 or 6 regiments to his right,
for the purpose of reinforcing him. I immediately ordered
forward a corresponding detachment.
The vigor of this movement gave evidence of the skill
and gallantry of the Genl commanding and the spirit
and courage of his men.
At the same time, I ordered the 46th Ills, Col. Davis,
to move forward, to the right and near to the road already
referred to, to support Genl. Wallace's left; and also ordered
Col Ross with the 3d Brigade of my Division to advance
directly on the same road - the object being to command the
space between Genl Wallace's left and my former position
on the ridge in front of the enemy's entrenchments. Col Ross

text: Office of Daily Toledo Blade AD PELTON CO Proprietors 150 Summit Street Toledo Ohio April 11 1868 Miss Dickinson May I put you to the trouble of informing me who can best arrange a lecture route making the arrangements in the New England States and also what compensation should be paid for such service I want to devote two months to New England next winter and prefer not to assume the labor of arranging routes I wound up the last season in Rochester NY Feb 27th to a spendid house My experience was pleasant throughout and I am really in love with the platform I shall have three lectures this winter I am receiving invitations daily many of which I owe to the kind words you have spoken of me Believe me I appreciate them Your friends Mr Mrs Camp are well I shall be in Philadelphia this summer Very truly yous D R Locke

text: FROM CHARLES MACGEACHY STURTEVANT HOUSE NEW YORK April 18 91 Dear Miss Dickinson I will undertake the management of your contemplated lecture tour this season and next commencing with the engagement at the Broadway Theatre this city on 26th instant Will arrange for you in other cities in the best obtainable theatres or halls Will pay all expenses of the tour including hotels carriages to and from hotels and theatres and railroad transportation of yourself and companion also myself and representative After deducting said expenses will divide evenly with you whatever surplus remains Settlements weekly You shall not be responsible for any deficit that may arise Box office statements and vouchers to be rendered to you at every accounting I am willing to serve you as above so long as mutually agreeable and advantageous Sincerely yours signature Miss Anna E Dickinson Sturtevant House New York N Y

Washington, Mar 4, 1862
Hon. E. M. Stanton
Secy War
I have known
the bearer of this letter, Mr. D.
K. Boswell, for nearly forty
years, and cheerfully commend
him as a gentleman
extremely worthy of confidence.
He has lived in the south
for several years, but from
what I have heard of him
through many friends and
relations of his in Indiana,
I feel fully warranted in vouching
for his loyalty and devotion
to the Union. I should
be pleased if you can consistent
with public duty assign him
to a responsible position
With the highest Respect
Yours truly
D.P. Hollosway

text: ROOMS OF THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE OF THE STATE IMPARTIAL SUFFRAGE ASSOCIATION Topeka Kansas April 5 1867 The Executive Committee of the State Impartial Suffrage Association desires to obtain the names of one or more earnest active friends of Impatial Suffrage with their Post Office address in each neighborhood in Kansas Will you furnish us at once with such a list in your County In addition we desire the names and address of every voter in your County to whom it wll do any good to send documents you can get such a list of your County Clerk or Township Trustees Correct and send it we want at least the names of half your voters We also want to know every neighborhood where it will do any good to hold meetings NB Blackwell and Lucy Stone are not canvassing the State and we have the promise of other speakers and intend before the next general election to reach every neighborhood and every voter Address SN WOOD Cor Sec State Impartial Suffrage Association Topeka Kansas PO Box 377

text:
Received in cipher
Washington Feb 28 '62
From Nashville 26th via Bowling Green 27:
Major Gen G.B. McClellan:
I arrived opposite the city with Mitchell's
division about nine thousand effective
on the night of the 24th. The enemy's cavalry
were still in the city in small
force - I did not intend to cross until
I could do so in sufficient force to run
no great hazard, but during the night
Gen. Nelson arrived with about seven
thousand men and landed before I was aware
of it. I deemed it unadvisable to withdraw
then lest it should embolden the enemy &
have a bad effect on the people & so determined
to cross with all the force at hand and
we are now crossing and taking a position
some four or five miles out in the
direction of Murfreesboro - The difficulty

text:
The World
FRIDAY, MARCH 7, 1862.
THE DAY'S NEWS.
[*14820-7*]
President Lincoln transmitted to Congress yesterday
a special message recommending the adoption
of the following joint resolution:
Resolved, That the United States ought to co-operate
with any state which may adopt a gradual
abolishment of slavery, giving to such state pecuniary
aid, to be used by such state in its discretion,
to compensate for the inconveniences, public and
private, produced by such change of system.
The President requests that, in case the resolution
meets the approval of Congress, the states and
people immediately interested be at once distinctly
notified of the fact so that they may begin
to consider whether to accept or reject it. He
also urges the measure as one of the most efficient
means of preserving the government.

2 CONSTRUCTION OF A SHIP CANAL.
Recent events in our relations with England impress upon us the importance of providing for such a contingency as the interruption of friendly relations with that power, but this we are prevented from doing by an agreement between our government and that of Great Britain, made in 1817, by which both are bound not to build or put afloat any armed vessels on the northern lakes, excepting two or three of small size, which agreement, however, may be abrogated by either party on giving six months' notice of its intention so to do.
Subsequently to the date of this agreement the St. Lawrence and the Welland canals were constructed with locks, and a depth of water sufficient to admit vessels of near two hundred feet in length and forty feet beam and nine feet draught of water to pass through, costing—. So that Great Britain has the power in a very short time to cover those lakes with war steamers built on the river St. Lawrence or in the ship-yards at home. To give notice of an intention to abrogate the agreement might at this present moment be unwise, and we are thus led to inquire whether any means may be found by which we can escape the disadvantages under which from changed circumstances that agreement places us. Manifestly by the opening of a channel from the lakes to navigable rivers flowing into the tide-water is the only way to regain equality with Great Britain.
Fortunately we have a channel already partially completed, by which, with improvement, armed vessels may be passed from the lakes to the ocean, and the reverse. This channel is the Illinois and Michigan canal, extending from Chicago to La Salle, on the Illinois river, ninety-six miles, and the bed of the river itself from that point to its mouth, where it flows into the Mississippi, 220 miles.
The value of the commerce on the Mississippi river and its tributaries is little less than that of the lakes. It extends over a distance of ten thousand miles of navigable waters, whose banks are covered at many points with valuable timber, rich in mines, studded with cities equal in building and manufacturing capacity to those on the lakes, and capable of constructing, as recent events have fully demonstrated, vessels of war of the most formidable character.
By the enlargement of this canal and the improvement of the navigation of the river, all the naval resources of the lakes can be transported to the Gulf of Mexico and to the ocean; and on the other hand, our naval forces on the ocean and on these rivers can be transported to the lakes, so as to quickly sweep all hostile fleets from their surface, and return again to tide-water. The importance of this channel in a purely naval point of view is so great that its expense would be more than saved, in one year of war with England, in the cost of vessels, while its value in protecting property, cities, and vessels, and in enabling us to uphold the honor of our flag, would be inestimable.
Again: the expense of transportation by water is so much less than that by railroad that, if extensive military operations are to be carried on, the saving to the government in this item would soon equal the entire cost of the work.
The government pays the railroads two cents per mile for the passage of each soldier, near six dollars from Chicago to St. Louis; one

text: Bay City Feb 3rd 1884 Dear Lolly Your letter is at hand and after A delay on account of sickness I desire to thank you for your very unnecessary apologies for I was sure you had A sad time and much correspondence to attend to tho I did fear I had given offence at my presumption that you would accept my invitation then again I did not know but that you needed the means of getting here and felt angry at myself for not delivering sending you tickets and then I heard you had left Detroit so did not know what to do now I am glad that I did not offend by my advice and indeed I meant all I said and it was the memory of A time when my darling was left by a dishonest manager far from Home

My whole command falling back, some four hundred
yards, from the left of their position in the morning,
the 2d Brigade was reformed, in line of battle, upon
ground that I had previously selected, at right angles
with their first line, to meet the contingency of the enemy's
approach from the position he had occupied in my rear.
The 1st Brigade was disposed in the rear of the 2d.
Here my men were supplied, both, with ammunition
and provisions, which had been brought up

Dispatching Capt Stewart of my staff and Capt
Dollins of the Cavalry, with instruction s to reconnoiter
the enemy and ascertain his strength and movements,
they found a large body of his forces falling back, in
apparent confusion, their officers vainly endeavoring to
bring them to a halt, and reported the fact. From another
position of the field, indications were observed in the
direction of the enemy's entrenchments of a hostile movement.
This was about 1 o'Clock P.M.
General Wallace, whose Division was formed near
the ground selected for my second line, filed it to the
right, and guided by Capt Stewart of my staff, formed
a portion of his fresh troops in front of my second line
and in close supporting distance of it - resting the

Washington City March 5th 1862
Dear Sir.
I drop you a short note. It is full
time for Mr. Boswell to be attended to in your
Department. The public interest involved is
most urgently pressing. Great service may be
immediately rendered in north Mississippi and
in north Alabama. Recruits from there are
now especially desirable. Mr Boswell has all the
credentials which a strong ardent man may need
We want first industry and energy , all subordinate
qualities will follow quite in abundance
I sincerely trust that you will
immediately start Mr Boswell to the scene
of his opperations.
Time is on the wing and precious
daylight is burning.
I write with pleasure to a prompt man
